analysis.one_liner: Requires a government-issued photo ID to vote in federal elections, with free voting-only IDs for people who cannot afford one.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House vote; it died at the end of the 112th Congress with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required anyone voting in a federal election to show a current, valid government-issued photo ID. In-person voters without one could cast only a provisional ballot and would have had to show the ID within 48 hours for it to count; mail voters would have to include a copy of the ID with the ballot (overseas active-duty military would be exempt). To soften the burden, states would have had to issue special photo IDs for voting at no charge to people who cannot afford the fee, with federal money covering those costs. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or any action beyond its initial committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the direct beneficiaries would be states (which receive federal payments to run the ID program) and voters who value stricter ID rules as a guard against impersonation fraud. Voters without existing photo ID would have gained access to a free voting-only ID. The bill's design — free IDs, fee waivers, and federal reimbursement — was aimed at blunting the usual objection that ID laws burden low-income voters.
analysis.who_benefits_short: States and voters seeking stricter ID rules

how_it_helps.text: It requires every voter in a federal election to present a current, valid government-issued photo ID — in person, by provisional ballot with ID shown within 48 hours, or by mail with a copy attached — which sponsors present as a safeguard of ballot integrity [S2][S3].

It requires every state to run a program providing free photo IDs for voting to people who lack them, waives the fee for people who attest they cannot afford it, and authorizes federal payments to cover those costs [S3].
It exempts overseas military voters on active duty from the mail-ballot photo ID requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, the cost would fall on voters who lack a government-issued photo ID — disproportionately low-income people, the elderly, and those without driver's licenses — who would have had to obtain a special voting-only ID or navigate the 48-hour provisional-ballot deadline. States would bear the administrative cost of running ID programs, offset by federal payments.

drawbacks.text: The bill makes a government-issued photo ID a precondition for voting: without one, an in-person voter can cast only a provisional ballot and must produce the ID within 48 hours or the ballot is not counted [S2][S3].
Mail and other non-in-person voters must submit a copy of photo ID with their ballot or it cannot be accepted, adding a step that can void a validly cast ballot [S3].
The free photo IDs the bill creates for voting cannot be used for any other government purpose, so a voter who gets one still lacks ID for other needs [S3].
The bill's own remedy depends on states building an ID-issuance program and on federal appropriations; if those fall short, eligible voters bear the consequences [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill did not become law, so the weighing is about what it would have done. It was more carefully built than many photo ID proposals: it required states to issue free voting-only IDs and reimbursed them for serving people who cannot afford the fee. But its core trade remains the same as in other voter ID laws: preventing a rare kind of fraud in exchange for adding a document requirement to voting, with the burden falling hardest on people without IDs and the risk that a 48-hour provisional-ballot deadline would count some valid votes out. Honest supporters would acknowledge the fraud it targets is rare; honest opponents would acknowledge the bill attempted to blunt the cost to poor voters. Because it never left committee, none of these trade-offs were tested in debate or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to a House committee and then to its Elections subcommittee, and it stayed there until the Congress ended — no hearings vote, no floor vote, ever.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Walsh (R-IL) introduced H.R. 5971 on June 19, 2012 [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the same day, and two days later to that committee's Subcommittee on Elections [S5].
No member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
No further action was recorded before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, so the bill died in committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained from the bill itself; it simply expired. Voters without photo ID were spared a new hurdle, and no state had to build the ID program it envisioned.

for.name: House Committee on House Administration / Subcommittee on Elections
for.what_they_did: Received the bill and never reported it out; it sat in the Elections subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Voters without government-issued photo ID (low-income, elderly, and others)
industries.note: The bill would have made a photo ID a condition of having a federal ballot counted, with a 48-hour window to cure a provisional ballot. The mitigating free-ID program makes it easier to comply, but the requirement itself is the cost.
States gain a new duty — and a new stream of federal payments — to issue voting-only photo IDs, expanding their role in election administration.

industries.industry: Absentee overseas military voters on active duty
industries.note: They are explicitly exempted from the mail-ballot photo ID requirement, keeping their existing process intact.
